title: Logic & Declarative Programming
summary: Programming by stating what's true or wanted and letting a solver find how — logic programming (Prolog) and declarative querying (SQL) as one family, unified by unification, backtracking, and hidden search cost.

slides.markdown:
Imperative code says *how*: loop through these rows, check this condition, accumulate this total. Functional code says *what*, as an expression to evaluate. **Declarative** code goes one step further — you describe *what you want*, or what relationships hold, and something else — a query planner, a logic engine — figures out how to produce it.

`SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30` never says "scan this table, compare each row." You describe the result; the database's query planner decides the actual execution strategy, and can change that strategy tomorrow without you touching the query.

Logic programming (Prolog) is declarative programming's purest form: you state facts and rules, then *ask questions*, and a search engine called unification-plus-backtracking finds every answer consistent with what you stated. This Topic covers both as one family, because the mental model — describe the goal, not the steps — is identical.

slides.sectionTitle: Describing the goal, not the steps
slides.markdown:
Every other paradigm in this group still tells the computer an order of operations, even functional code (evaluate the innermost expression first, then the next). Declarative programming removes that requirement entirely: you assert relationships that hold, and a separate solver is responsible for finding *some* sequence of steps that satisfies them.

Concretely: "sort this list" imperatively means writing a comparison-and-swap loop. Declaratively, in SQL, it means `ORDER BY column` — you never specify quicksort or mergesort; you assert the desired property (ascending order) and the engine picks an algorithm, possibly a different one depending on data size or an index that exists.

This is exactly why the same declarative statement can run differently across engines, or across versions of the same engine, without you changing a line — the *what* is fixed, the *how* is the implementation's problem to solve, and it's allowed to get better without your code changing.

slides.subTitle: Prolog-style unification
slides.markdown:
A logic program has two kinds of statements. A **fact** asserts something unconditionally true: `parent(tom, bob).` says Tom is a parent of Bob, full stop. A **rule** asserts something conditionally true: `grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).` says X is Z's grandparent *if* X is some Y's parent and Y is Z's parent.

Neither a fact nor a rule computes anything by itself — they're a database of relationships. Computation happens when you **query**: `?- grandparent(tom, W).` asks "for what W is Tom a grandparent of W?" and the engine searches the facts and rules for every W that makes the rule's right-hand side true.

This is the declarative core: you never wrote a loop that walks the parent relationships looking for grandchildren. You wrote down what "grandparent" *means*, and the engine works out which specific facts satisfy that meaning.

Given `parent(tom, bob).`, `parent(bob, ann).`, `parent(bob, pat).`, and the grandparent rule from the previous Subtopic, the query `?- grandparent(tom, W).` doesn't jump straight to an answer — it searches.

The engine tries to satisfy `parent(tom, Y)` first, finds `Y = bob` (the only match), then tries to satisfy `parent(bob, Z)` with that `Y` bound — finds `Z = ann`, returns `W = ann` as a first answer. If you ask for more solutions, the engine **backtracks**: it undoes the last binding (`Z = ann`), tries the next alternative for `parent(bob, Z)`, finds `Z = pat`, and returns `W = pat`.

That undo-and-retry-the-next-alternative loop is backtracking, and it's the search engine behind every Prolog query — a systematic exploration of the space of variable bindings that could make the goal true, abandoning (backtracking out of) any branch that fails and trying the next.

slides.sectionTitle: Unification and backtracking as the engine
slides.markdown:
Two mechanisms do all the work in logic programming, and neither exists in imperative or functional code in the same form.

**Unification** is the process of finding values for variables that make two terms match. Matching `parent(tom, Y)` against the fact `parent(tom, bob)` unifies `Y` with `bob` — it's more general than plain assignment because it can bind variables on *either* side, and it can fail (matching `parent(tom, Y)` against `parent(sue, bob)` fails outright, no binding exists).

**Backtracking** is what happens when a chosen unification leads to a dead end later in the search: the engine retracts the binding and tries the next possible unification instead, exploring the search space depth-first.

Together, they turn a declarative statement ("grandparent is defined as...") into an actual computation: unification proposes candidate bindings, backtracking systematically explores all of them until the query is satisfied or the search space is exhausted. This search-based execution model is the real distinguishing feature of logic programming — no other paradigm in this group runs your program by exploring a space of possibilities.

```prolog
parent(tom, bob).
parent(bob, ann).
parent(bob, pat).

grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).

?- grandparent(tom, W).
% W = ann ;
% W = pat.
```

Nothing here is a loop or a branch in the imperative sense. `grandparent(X, Z) :- parent(X, Y), parent(Y, Z).` reads as "X is Z's grandparent if there's some Y such that X is Y's parent and Y is Z's parent" — a definition, not a procedure. The `?-` line is the only thing that *asks* for computation; everything above it is pure declaration.

Running the query, Prolog's engine finds both `ann` and `pat` by unifying and backtracking exactly as traced in the previous Subtopics — you never wrote the search, you only wrote what a valid answer looks like.

slides.subTitle: What vs how
slides.markdown:
SQL is the declarative language most engineers already use daily, and recognizing it as declarative is the point of pairing it with Prolog in this Topic. `SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30 ORDER BY name` states *what* rows you want and in what order — it never says whether to scan the whole table or use an index on `age`, and it never says whether to sort with a merge sort or a heap sort.

The database's **query planner** is the "solver" here, playing the same role Prolog's unification engine plays for a logic query: given the declarative statement, it works out a concrete execution plan (a *how*) and can pick a different plan tomorrow — a new index appears, statistics change, a new planner version ships — without your SQL changing at all.

This is exactly the same relationship as facts-and-rules-vs-query in Prolog: your `WHERE` clause is a condition to satisfy, not a loop to execute, and the engine is free to satisfy it however is fastest.

slides.subTitle: Describing constraints, not a search
slides.markdown:
Constraint programming pushes the declarative idea into optimization problems: instead of writing a search algorithm for, say, a valid Sudoku grid, you state the constraints — each row has digits 1-9 with no repeats, each column the same, each 3x3 box the same — and a **constraint solver** searches for an assignment satisfying all of them simultaneously.

The solver is doing the same kind of work Prolog's backtracking search does, but specialized: modern solvers use techniques like constraint propagation (immediately ruling out impossible values once a neighboring cell is fixed) to prune the search space far more aggressively than naive backtracking, which is why they can solve problems (large scheduling problems, bin-packing) that a hand-written backtracking loop would take impractically long on.

The declarative payoff is the same as SQL's: you describe the rules once, and the solver's search strategy can improve without you rewriting anything about what a valid solution looks like.

slides.sectionTitle: A sorting rule vs a loop
slides.markdown:
| | Imperative sort | Declarative sort |
|---|---|---|
| **What you write** | A comparison-and-swap loop (or a call to one) | `ORDER BY column` / a sortedness constraint |
| **What you specify** | The exact algorithm and its steps | The property the result must satisfy |
| **Who picks the algorithm** | You | The engine — can change without your code changing |
| **Debugging a wrong order** | Step through the loop's comparisons | Check the stated property (collation, null ordering) matches intent |

The declarative version is shorter and, when it's wrong, wrong in a different way: a bug in `ORDER BY name` is almost never an algorithmic bug (the sort itself is correct) — it's a specification bug, like forgetting `name` is case-sensitive or that nulls sort first by default. Declarative code moves the class of bugs you'll hit from "my steps were wrong" to "my stated requirement didn't mean what I thought."

slides.subTitle: Hidden search cost
slides.markdown:
Declarative code's biggest trap is that brevity hides cost instead of eliminating it. A one-line SQL query with a `JOIN` across three unindexed million-row tables can trigger a search (effectively a nested-loop scan) that's dramatically slower than an equally short-looking query with the right indexes — and the source code gives you no visual signal of which one you wrote.

Same in Prolog: a recursive rule with a subtle ordering mistake can cause the backtracking search to explore exponentially many dead-end branches before finding (or failing to find) an answer, even though the rule reads as a compact, obviously-correct statement of the relationship.

The senior instinct here: for declarative code, "is this correct" and "is this fast" are answered by looking at *different things entirely* — correctness by reading the statement, performance by inspecting the query plan (`EXPLAIN` in SQL) or the solver's search behavior, never by eyeballing how short the code is. Short and slow, and short and fast, look identical on the page.
